archetype.name: Game Manager (under-center backup)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup who, in Seattle's run-leaning offense, works mostly short and intermediate off under-center looks and feeds his No. 1 receiver, a far tighter version of the turnover-prone, inaccurate passer his career line describes.

report.headline: Two sharp games built on Smith-Njigba and under-center throws, not a new Lock.
report.take:
Start with what the dossier can and can't tell us. His 2026 stat line comes from two games, Week 1 against New England and a Week 2 start at Arizona. The start log credits him with Weeks 2 through 6, yet no stat lines from those later weeks are included. As of October 20 he is listed as QB2 and was limited in practice in Week 6. So the 0.451 EPA per dropback (2nd of 45) and 6.72 CPOE (3rd) are real numbers on a 48-attempt base, and they belong to a player who is not currently the starter. The team's passing EPA ranks 19th of 32, which suggests Seattle's passing game as a whole has been nowhere near as efficient as those two games.

What drove the two games is clear. Jaxon Smith-Njigba drew 21 targets at 1.178 EPA each, and those targets alone add up to more EPA than all of Lock's dropbacks combined. Everyone else was close to neutral or worse, with Rashid Shaheed at -0.451 per target. The other driver was formation. Under center he went 100% with a 0.891 EPA per play and an 80% success rate. From shotgun the success rate fell to 37.1%, the CPOE to -2.5 and the completion rate to 61.8%. Seattle passes 5.4 points less than expected (27th), and the run game is 30th. In that offense, defenses have to respect the run, so play action and under-center throws open up while pure dropback passing does not.

The career line is the reality check. He has posted a negative CPOE in every season on record, including -6.1 with the Giants in 2024 and -5.5 in his 2020 starting year, when he threw 15 interceptions (58th of 59). His bad-throw rate has usually landed in the bottom half. Zero interceptions, a deep line of five attempts at 1.971 EPA, and a +6.7 CPOE over 48 throws are not enough to overturn five seasons of evidence. The shotgun split, his one sample that looks like a normal dropback passer's workload, is where he looks most like the career version.

Where it's heading: for now he is a backup, and the depth chart move matters more than any efficiency stat. If he plays again, expect a competent, conservative passer who leans on Smith-Njigba and the run-game structure. Expect him to be closer to league average than to the top-three rate stats, with interceptions returning at something near his career rate.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba with confidence
strengths.body: Lock's production runs almost entirely through one receiver. Smith-Njigba's targets generated more EPA than all of Lock's dropbacks combined, at better than a point per target. That is a sound process for a backup: find the best separator and trust him. It lasts only as long as the top receiver keeps winning, and it says more about Smith-Njigba than about Lock.

strengths.title: Efficient off under-center looks
strengths.body: Under center he completed every attempt, with an 80% success rate and 0.891 EPA per play. This is the scheme doing its job: a run-leaning offense pulls linebackers up and leaves defined windows. The exact numbers will come down, but the edge from these looks should hold as long as Seattle keeps playing this way.

strengths.title: Rate stats near the top
strengths.body: Across two games his EPA per dropback, adjusted net yards per dropback and TD rate all rank second among 45 qualifiers, with no turnovers. These are real results against a 17th-ranked and a 28th-ranked defense. They are a two-game peak, not a baseline.

concerns.title: Career accuracy says regression is coming
concerns.body: He has posted a negative CPOE every season on record, and his 2020 starting year produced 15 interceptions. A +6.7 CPOE on 48 attempts, with five deep throws inflating the EPA, is a hot streak against weaker defenses rather than a new skill. Expect accuracy and turnover luck to move back toward his history.

concerns.title: Ordinary when asked to drop back
concerns.body: From shotgun his success rate fell to 37.1% and his CPOE turned negative. When the formation doesn't help him, he looks like the passer his career describes. If game script forces Seattle into obvious passing downs, his efficiency will likely fall off.

concerns.title: Now the backup behind a weak line
concerns.body: He is listed as QB2 as of October 20, so playing time is the first problem. Whoever plays sits behind a line ranked last in hit rate allowed. Lock was hit or sacked on 16% of his dropbacks even in favorable spots.

trend.note: In the two logged games he improved from 6.4 EPA against New England to 16.1 at Arizona, his only listed start. The dossier has no stat lines after that, and he now sits second on the depth chart, so the path is two good data points followed by a demotion.

nextGame.headline: Stingy short defense and a WR1 lockdown, if he plays at all
nextGame.body:
Kansas City is a poor fit for how Lock has won. Its defense ranks 3rd overall and allows -0.261 EPA on short passes (2nd stingiest), and most of his throws have come under 10 air yards. It has also been the stingiest defense in the league per target against opposing WR1s, which hits a passer whose value has come almost entirely from Smith-Njigba. The openings are elsewhere. Kansas City gets little pressure, with a sack rate ranked 27th. It has been only middling on deep balls, and it gives up a lot to tight ends, both in target share and in points over average for TE1s. Seattle is a 2.5-point home favorite with a 42.5 total, which points to a low-scoring game the Seahawks' defense can keep close.

The first question is whether Lock plays. He is QB2 on the October 20 depth chart, so this outlook applies only if he starts or comes in. Seattle's side has some help coming: guard Anthony Bradford has been designated to return from IR, and Zach Charbonnet has a good chance to play. Either would lift a 30th-ranked run game and a line that allows hits at the league's worst rate. Jadarian Price remains out, and tight end Elijah Arroyo is out for significant time, which leaves AJ Barner to attack Kansas City's soft spot at tight end. On Kansas City's side, Rashee Rice is out, Tyquan Thornton is on IR and two tackles are banged up, which could dull an offense that ranks 4th and help Seattle keep a neutral, run-heavy script.

keyMatchups.title: Smith-Njigba against a WR1 lockdown
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City has allowed the lowest EPA per target to WR1s in the league, and Lock's whole passing profile runs through his WR1. If Smith-Njigba is contained, nothing else in Lock's 2026 target tree has carried an offense.

keyMatchups.title: Short game into a strong short defense
keyMatchups.body: Lock's offense lives under 10 air yards, and Kansas City allows the second-lowest EPA on short throws. The cleaner path is deeper. Kansas City's deep defense is middling, and its weak pass rush should give him time on play action.

keyMatchups.title: Barner against a soft TE defense
keyMatchups.body: With Arroyo out, Barner is the tight end, and Kansas City has let TE1s score 3.5 PPR over their averages (27th). Its share of targets to tight ends also runs well above the league's. This is the likeliest secondary outlet.

nextGame.watch: Who takes the first snap. If it's Lock, watch whether Seattle keeps him under center with Charbonnet back, or puts him in shotgun, where his numbers have looked like his career.

restOfSeason.body:
Treat Lock as a backup with a strong two-game sample. If he gets more starts, the parts likely to last are the structure: a run-leaning, under-center offense, a top receiver who wins, and a short-to-intermediate approach that keeps sacks manageable. What will regress is the accuracy and turnover luck. He has never posted a positive CPOE in a season on record, and zero interceptions on a career-long gunslinger profile won't hold. In any start, expect something like 180-235 passing yards and a touchdown or so, with interceptions coming back. That is a competent spot starter, not a top-five rate passer.

The ceiling depends on Smith-Njigba staying dominant and the line improving with Bradford back. The floor is a game against a strong defense where Seattle has to drop back, which is where his shotgun numbers have looked like his career.
swingFactors: Whether he regains or keeps a starting role
Bradford and Charbonnet returning to steady the run game and protection

confidence.note: The season line rests on two games and 48 attempts. He is now QB2, his career profile points the other way, and the dossier's start log and stat lines don't fully match.
